Update: Confirmed AppState init runs several synchronous migrations and history loads on the main thread and that SystemAudioClassifier.startSoundClassification ends up rebuilding the AVAudioSession/engine at first launch; preparing root-cause summary.

**Ranked root causes**

1. **Cold-start audio session + engine setup still blocks the UI even though it’s dispatched to a background queue.**  
   `AppState.restartDetection` fires immediately when the Home tab first appears (it sets `soundDetectionIsRunning = true`, builds thresholds, and calls `SystemAudioClassifier.shared.startSoundClassification(...)` while the “loading audio” overlay is shown).  `GlobalDetection/appstate.swift:314-374`  
   `startSoundClassification` then rebuilds the entire audio stack: it creates an `SNClassifySoundRequest`, installs an `SNAudioStreamAnalyzer`, and calls `startAnalyzing`, which itself calls `startAudioSession` (category changes plus `setActive(false/true)`) before wiping and restarting the `AVAudioEngine`.  `GlobalDetection/SystemAudioClassifier.swift:935-987` and `GlobalDetection/SystemAudioClassifier.swift:820-860`  
   Even though the work runs on a background QoS queue, each `setActive`/`setCategory` call blocks for ~2–3 seconds when the audio session is first acquired, so the first launch feels sluggish. After the app is backgrounded/foregrounded, `resumeAudioEngine` simply restarts an already-initialized engine, so the latency disappears.

2. **AppState’s init runs a bucket of synchronous migrations and history loading on the main thread before the UI renders.**  
   The initializer evaluates several `UserDefaults` flags, writes new defaults, walks large sound sets (`SoundCatalog.defaultLabels`), and only afterward calls `loadDetectionHistoryFromStorage`.  `GlobalDetection/appstate.swift:88-220`  
   All of that happens before the first view hierarchy mounts, so the main run-loop is held up on launch. After backgrounding and returning, `init` has already run, so these migrations do not re-execute and the launch path is faster.

3. **Loading detection history blocks on a serial cache queue + JSON decode until the first background task flush, then stays fast.**  
   `loadDetectionHistoryFromStorage` takes the initial taps history by calling `SharedStorage.getTapsHistory()`, which synchronously locks `cacheQueue`, decodes `tapsHistoryData`, and populates `cachedTapsHistory`.  `GlobalDetection/appstate.swift:198-204` and `GlobalDetection/SharedStorage.swift:125-145`  
   If the persisted history is non-trivial, that decode runs on the main thread during launch, contributing to the startup stall. After the initial decode, `cachedTapsHistory` is populated, so later foreground transitions read from the cache without the decode, which is why the lag goes away after the app has already run once.

**Next steps**
1. Profile the cold launch with Instruments (Time Profiler + Activity Monitor) to measure how long `startAudioSession`/`setActive` blocks the main thread and verify the JSON decode duration.
2. Consider deferring noncritical migrations/historical loads to a background queue or split them into smaller ticks so the first frame isn’t blocked.
3. Keep the audio stack warmed by reusing the analyzer/audio engine as early as possible (e.g., avoid tearing it down entirely when the app first launches) so that background/foreground transitions don’t have to rebuild anything heavy.
